stories.headline: Houston Mayor Orders Police to Limit Cooperation With ICE After Democratic Midterm Wins in Texas
stories.summary:
Houston Mayor John Whitmire, a Democrat, issued an executive order on Friday directing the city's police to limit cooperation with federal immigration officials. The move comes days after Democrats won a series of stunning victories in Texas in the midterm elections, including the governorship and a U.S. Senate seat. It breaks with policy set by Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid to Gina Hinojosa.

Under the new rules, Houston officers will contact ICE only if a person arrested for a jailable offense also has an administrative ICE warrant, which is issued internally by the Department of Homeland Security. Police Chief Noe Diaz said someone stopped for a minor traffic infraction and given a citation will simply go on their way. Previously, officers were required to notify ICE whenever a search of the National Crime Information Center database showed such a warrant.

Whitmire said he acted "to begin a healing process" and "reduce fear and anxiety across our community," adding, "elections matter." Months of public outcry in Houston followed an ICE officer's fatal shooting of a man who was driving to work. Whitmire also urged Congress to require better training, body cameras and de-escalation instruction for ICE, saying such changes can only come from Washington.

A DHS spokesperson said the department remains "disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE," arguing that partnerships with local law enforcement are critical to arresting what it called criminal illegal aliens. Austin has begun implementing a similar change. Democrats won both chambers of Congress on Tuesday, and Texas elected its first Democratic governor since 1995 and its first Democratic senator since 1988.

stories.headline: Italy's Foreign Minister Says Pro-Russian Hackers Leaked His Personal Data
stories.summary:
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said cyber-criminals have spent days publishing his personal data on the dark web and seeking more information, exposing him and his family to new threats and intimidation. He did not specify the nature of the threats. Tajani, who is also deputy prime minister, wrote on X that his government's position on Ukraine is the political reason he was targeted.

He said defending the freedom of a sovereign state and taking a clear stand for its democracy and independence is seen as dangerous by such criminal entities. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni blamed pro-Russian hackers and offered Tajani her full solidarity. She said the sale of confidential information about institutional representatives is a serious concern that must be tackled with the utmost determination.

Meloni also voiced concern about the circulation of false images that she said were shared by members of Italy's opposition, without giving details. Moscow has not publicly responded to the allegations. Italy has provided humanitarian and military support to Ukraine in its war with Russia. The incident follows other recent cyber incidents in Europe, including an attack on shop freezers in seven countries.

stories.headline: Houthis Say at Least 25 Killed in Saudi Air Strike in Yemen
stories.summary:
Media linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen say at least 25 people, including women and children, were killed in air strikes carried out by Saudi Arabia. Footage on the Houthi-run Al Masirah television station showed rescuers pulling bodies, including those of young children, from the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town east of the capital, Sanaa. The Houthi-run Saba news agency attributed the attack to Saudi Arabia. There has been no comment from the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government.

The strike came hours after the coalition said it intercepted a missile heading toward Riyadh. Houthi leader Mahdi al-Mashat has vowed that the group will take revenge for the latest attacks. On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province reportedly killed 30 people; the Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia, while government forces said the Houthis had fired a missile at the site.

The war in Yemen had been dormant for several years but reignited as a result of the Iran war. A truce began to unravel when Saudi Arabia struck the Houthi-controlled Sanaa airport to prevent an Iranian plan from landing there. The Houthis then targeted Abha airport in Saudi Arabia and began hitting Saudi ships using the Red Sea as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz. The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.

stories.headline: Update: US Offers $20 Million Reward for Information on Iran's Nuclear Program
stories.summary:
The US State Department's Rewards for Justice program announced a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear program, including its "facilities, equipment and associated personnel." The program also offered to potentially relocate the person who provides such details. The department said Iran's lack of compliance with the International Atomic Energy Agency on safeguards has led the agency to lose "continuity of knowledge" about Iran's production and inventory of key components such as centrifuges.

Separately, US Central Command said it is setting up Task Force Iron Gate, based in Tampa, Florida, to restrict Iran's movement of weapons, dual-use goods and illegal revenue across its borders. Centcom estimates its naval blockade of Iranian ports has prevented Iran from exporting more than $25 billion in crude oil. Iran insists its nuclear program is peaceful and says it has no intention of developing a nuclear weapon.

The announcements come after midterm elections in which both President Trump and Vice President JD Vance acknowledged that public opposition to the war fueled heavy Republican losses, prompting speculation the White House may not seek escalation. Before the vote, Trump said the US might need to go after the underground site known as Pickaxe Mountain. On Friday he said Iran wants "to make a deal very badly." Qatar's foreign ministry said both sides were reviewing proposals it has presented.

stories.headline: Promising Experimental Heart Disease Drug Fails to Reduce Heart Attacks in Trial
stories.summary:
An experimental drug that lowers lipoprotein(a), a common risk factor for heart attacks, failed to deliver the expected benefit in a clinical trial. Doctors had expected the medicine to save patients' lives, but it made no difference in outcomes.

Elevated lipoprotein(a) is a genetically driven risk factor affecting a substantial share of the population, and drugmakers have invested heavily in therapies to reduce it. The result is a notable setback for that approach.

The finding raises questions about whether lowering the marker alone is sufficient to prevent cardiovascular events, and researchers are likely to examine the data further.

stories.headline: Gunman Opens Fire in Krakow's Main Square, Killing 6 and Wounding 15
stories.summary:
Six people were killed and 15 wounded on Saturday afternoon after a gunman opened fire in the busy Main Square of Krakow, Poland, authorities said. The Malopolski regional government raised the death toll from five to six in a post on X. Police officers are among the wounded.

Krakow police said the attacker, a Polish citizen, aimed at random people after driving into the square, one of Poland's major tourist destinations. He was wearing military-style fatigues and used a military-type long gun. He was shot and wounded in a gunfight with officers a short distance from the initial violence. Police found many other weapons and ammunition in his car.

Police spokesperson Katarzyna Cislo told TVN24 that the gunman acted alone and that the public is safe. A tram driver had reported around 3 p.m. that a man in a moving car shot at his vehicle near the square, shattering the window of the driver's cabin. Around 15 million tourists visit Krakow each year, most of them passing through the Main Square, and mass shootings are uncommon in Poland.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk said police are investigating, and President Karol Nawrocki said his thoughts were with the victims, the wounded and their families. U.S. Ambassador Tom Rose called the attack a savage and murderous assault and said America stands with Poland. Authorities have not yet released a motive or the gunman's identity.

stories.headline: Barnier Warns UK It Cannot 'Cherry Pick' Single Market Access as Burnham Eyes Closer EU Ties
stories.summary:
Michel Barnier, the EU's former Brexit negotiator, warned that the United Kingdom cannot pick and choose which parts of the single market it joins. Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he said there is no single market a la carte menu. He was responding to Prime Minister Andy Burnham's stated wish to explore closer economic ties with Europe.

Barnier said EU members would require the UK to accept the bloc's four freedoms, covering goods, services, capital and people, including free movement. He said there will be no possibility of having one freedom and not the others. He added that the door is open within Europe for the UK to rejoin as a full member.

Burnham, prime minister since July, has suggested Labour could pursue a much closer relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the bloc, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election. He recently said he would not restore free movement without a referendum, and Downing Street clarified he was not advocating its return at this point. Free movement was a central issue in the 2016 referendum, and any move toward it would be a key dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK.

Both sides hope to use a Brussels meeting in 10 days to unveil deals on food standards, youth visas and linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime.

stories.headline: Germany Expects Fighter Jet Partnership Decision by March After FCAS Collapse
stories.summary:
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius expects a decision by the end of March 2027 on a new air combat partnership to jointly build a next-generation fighter jet. He made the comments in an interview with the Funke media group, according to Bloomberg.

The timeline follows the scrapping of the Franco-German Future Combat Air System, known as FCAS, earlier this year. The collapse of the project left Germany seeking new partners for a sixth-generation fighter program.

The decision will shape European military aviation and defense industry cooperation for decades. Details on which countries or companies Germany is considering were not included in the initial report.

stories.headline: Update: Russian Missile and Drone Barrage Hits Ukraine's Power Grid Ahead of Abu Dhabi Talks
stories.summary:
Russia launched more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones against Ukraine overnight, damaging energy infrastructure and causing blackouts and water disruptions, President Volodymyr Zelensky said. Twelve regions came under attack, with Kyiv hit hardest. Nine people were reported hurt nationwide, including one child, according to the BBC; Bloomberg reported at least one civilian killed in the Kyiv area.

Zelensky said residential buildings, the North Bridge and a kindergarten were damaged in the capital, and that substations linking the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine were struck. Substations were also damaged in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply had returned to normal and about 60 percent of apartment buildings were reconnected to heating. Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said five regions had power cuts. Temperatures are falling, and parts of the country have seen the first winter snow.

The attacks came before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to attend trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week. Zelensky wrote on Telegram that Moscow was preparing for the talks by targeting critical infrastructure, and said Ukraine counts on bipartisan U.S. support, including increased sanctions pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The strikes followed a White House event on Thursday at which First Lady Melania Trump hosted both delegations and urged a more enduring ceasefire, after a six-day truce allowed hundreds of residents to evacuate the occupied town of Oleshky. Earlier this week, glide bomb strikes on an aid centre near Zaporizhzhia killed at least 55 people.

stories.headline: No Clear Winner After Tight New Zealand General Election
stories.summary:
New Zealand's general election on Saturday produced no clear winner, and the leaders of the two major parties are preparing for coalition negotiations. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats in preliminary results, 19 short of a simple majority despite being the largest party. With coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, the governing bloc would hold a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal can be struck.

Opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, did not concede, saying the shape of the next government will remain uncertain for a while. He said the next parliament will require compromise and common ground. Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a very hard-fought race. More than 99 percent of votes have been counted, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in vote share.

Preliminary results showed historically low support for the two major parties, at a combined 60 percent or so. The Opportunity Party crossed the 5 percent threshold to enter parliament for the first time and is seen as a possible kingmaker; leader Qiulae Wong said it would work with either side but negotiate first with the party winning the most seats. The Greens, who campaigned on forcing the two main supermarket chains to divest stores, also gained support.

The campaign was shaped by the cost of living and unemployment. Special votes, including those cast overseas, will be counted over the next three weeks, and the electoral commission will announce official results on 27 November. Professor Andrew Geddis of the University of Otago said the outcome could come down to very fine margins in individual electorates.

stories.headline: US Military Creates Special Unit to Block Iran's Land Routes for Arms Shipments
stories.summary:
The U.S. military said it is creating a special unit to help block the land routes Iran uses to transport advanced weapons and other materials, according to Bloomberg. The announcement marks a new effort to disrupt Iranian arms flows beyond maritime and air interdiction.

The move comes amid an intense period in U.S.-Iran relations. Recent coverage has described U.S. defensive strikes on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, satellite images showing Iran rebuilding near missile bases, and a behind-the-scenes push led by Vice President JD Vance for a new ceasefire and nuclear talks. President Trump has been weighing a deal or renewed strikes, and the Iran war became a central issue after the midterm elections.

Details on the unit's size, composition, command and the specific routes targeted were not provided in the initial report. Supporters of a tougher posture argue that cutting supply lines constrains Iran and its partners without a wider escalation, while critics of the war, including many Democrats who won in the midterms, have urged diplomacy and congressional oversight of military actions. Further details are expected from the Pentagon.

stories.headline: US Officials Believe Woman Close to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Was a Chinese Spy, NYT Reports
stories.summary:
U.S. intelligence officials told the Trump administration that a woman who had become close to Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang was working for a Chinese spy agency, which recruited her to collect information on him, the New York Times reported Friday. Bloomberg relayed the report on Saturday.

The account, which has not been independently confirmed in the material available, raises questions about the targeting of top technology executives by foreign intelligence services. Nvidia makes the advanced chips at the center of the artificial intelligence boom and of U.S. export controls aimed at limiting China's access to the technology.

The report comes during a volatile stretch for technology shares, with the Nasdaq falling more than 5.5 percent after the midterm elections. Neither Nvidia nor Chinese authorities were quoted in the initial summary. Further responses from the company, the White House and Beijing are likely.

stories.headline: Update: Paraguay's President Peña Impeached Unanimously and Placed Under House Arrest After Bank Collapse
stories.summary:
Paraguay's Senate voted 44-0 on Friday to impeach President Santiago Peña over the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests. One senator was absent. Peña was arrested minutes after the vote. He had offered to resign on Thursday, but senators declined to accept the resignation and instead impeached and charged him with misconduct. That decision strips him of the immunity usually granted to former presidents.

The charges allege conflicts of interest, manipulation of regulatory oversight, diversion of pension funds, and participation in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank. Peña held shares in the company that owned the bank until last year. He has denied wrongdoing. His lawyer, Ricardo Preda, called the allegations a reckless accusation. Prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said Peña is due to be questioned on Saturday over alleged breach of trust, influence peddling and misappropriation of funds.

Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as interim president and will serve until 2028. He pledged that affected depositors will be fully compensated. An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions after the central bank seized Ueno, leaving more than half the population cut off from accounts. Protests have spread nationwide, with earlier clashes in which police used tear gas and water cannons.

Senator Rafael Filizzola called the affair the biggest corruption scandal in Paraguay's democratic history. Analysts expect Peña to be prosecuted over the bank's failure. The key questions now are how and when depositors will be repaid and whether the unrest subsides under the new government.

stories.headline: Cornell Faculty Senate Passes No-Confidence Vote Over Handling of Sexual Assault Allegations
stories.summary:
Cornell University's faculty senate voted 75 to 50 on Friday to express no confidence in the central administration's ability to address what it called an ongoing crisis of sexual assault on campus. The vote follows a lawsuit by a former student, identified as Jane Doe, who alleges she was gang raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. The resolution is largely symbolic because the senate cannot remove university leaders.

All seven accused men have denied wrongdoing, and none has been charged. Doe reported the incident to campus police, but the local prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time. She has accused President Michael Kotlikoff of asking why she waited several weeks to report, an account the university says is incorrect.

The board of trustees, which has the power to fire Kotlikoff, said it remains confident in him and his administration. Chairwoman Anne Meinig Smalling said the vote reflects deep anger across campus and that what happened to Doe is unacceptable. Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said he believes the senate did not act lightly and hopes the vote helps address the longstanding problem.

Cornell initially defended its disciplinary measures but has since acknowledged it fell short in handling the case. It has hired a former attorney general to conduct an independent review and has announced further measures on assault. Backlash has been intense since Doe filed suit in September.

stories.headline: Dozens of Democrats Weighing 2028 Presidential Bids, Former Obama Campaign Chief Says
stories.summary:
Jim Messina, who ran Barack Obama's 2012 re-election campaign, said more than two dozen Democrats are actively considering 2028 White House runs after the party's strong midterm showing. He told the BBC's Americast podcast he has spoken with over two dozen campaigns that have begun fundraising and hiring staff. He expects exploratory committees to be announced in coming weeks, likely after Thanksgiving.

Messina credited the party's gains to a disciplined focus on the economy and the impact of President Donald Trump's tariffs, which he said hurt rural voters. He said Democrats flipped seats in traditionally Republican states such as Iowa, Kansas and Texas by avoiding what he called social wars. Republicans have not been quoted in this account, and Messina is a partisan Democratic voice whose assessment reflects his own view.

He cautioned that the results were not a ringing endorsement of the party, saying the MVP of the election for Democrats was Trump. He predicted the field could shrink as candidates face the pressure of raising large sums. The harder task, he said, will be uniting the party's progressive and centrist wings in Congress.

Messina said candidates will need a clear economic vision and a position on artificial intelligence, and must decide whether to focus on Trump daily. He called the coming race the most interesting presidential election since 2008.

stories.headline: Jehovah's Witnesses Reverse Blood Transfusion Ban Weeks After Texas Man's Death
stories.summary:
The Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body announced a major doctrinal change in September, ending the prohibition on most medical procedures using donated blood. Decisions on such treatments are now left to individual believers. The ban dated to 1945 and rested on interpretations of Bible verses requiring abstention from blood.

The change came 23 days after the death of Isaac Valdez, 26, of Waxahachie, Texas. In August he suffered an epileptic seizure at a library and a resulting brain haemorrhage. As a Witness he carried a No Blood card, and his family honored his wishes when a neurosurgeon said an emergency operation requiring transfusion was the only way to save him. He died on 26 August when life support was withdrawn.

His twin brother, Jacob Valdez, said he is angry that leaders did not reach the decision sooner and believes Isaac could still be alive. Church leaders describe the change as applying Bible principles to modern medicine, though it follows years of pressure from within and outside the faith. The Governing Body is based in New York state.
